title: Tunable g-Factors of Hybridized Orbitals in a Quantum Dot Molecule
authors: Michelle Lienhart, Krzysztof Gawarecki, Pavel Daskalov, Christopher Thalacker, Nadeem Akhlaq, Irina Ivanova, Johannes Schall, Sven Rodt, Stephan Reitzenstein, Arne Ludwig, Dirk Reuter, Kai Müller, Jonathan J. Finley
abstract: The ability to control the $g$-factors of orbital spin states in optically active quantum dot molecules (QDMs) is a prerequisite for the high-fidelity generation of multi-photonic cluster states with higher-dimensional entanglement structure. Protocols that rely on two coupled spins require knowledge of the $g$-factor and its dependence on external control parameters. Mismatches in the $g$-factor between tunnel-coupled dots introduce unwanted dephasing of coupled spin-states, making precise characterization and voltage control essential. Here, we measure the gate voltage dependence of the electron and hole $g$-factors of negatively charged trions $X^{-}$ in a single InGaAs QDM using polarization-resolved magneto-photoluminescence spectroscopy. The electron $g$-factor exhibits a pronounced step-like change at the tunneling resonance, shifting from $g_\mathrm{e} = -0.336\pm 0.008$ to $g_\mathrm{e} = -0.389\pm 0.003$, providing a direct spectroscopic fingerprint of molecular orbital formation and a shift of the wavefunction localization from the lower to the upper dot. In contrast, the hole $g$-factor remains nearly constant at $g_\mathrm{h} \approx 0.094 \pm 0.007$, exhibiting a weak modulation near the anticrossing voltages attributed to Coulomb-mediated deformation of the wavefunction by the tunneling electron. Our results are quantitatively reproduced by an eight-band $\mathbf{k}{\cdot}\mathbf{p}$ model, establishing electric-field control of the trion $g$-factors as a practical tool for independently tuning the Zeeman splitting of individual dots and opening new pathways towards the deterministic generation of two-dimensional photonic cluster states.
summary: This work demonstrates the ability to electrically tune the electron and hole g-factors within a quantum dot molecule using magneto-photoluminescence spectroscopy. By observing distinct changes in $g_e$ at tunneling resonances, the authors confirm that electric fields provide precise control over spin properties. This capability opens new pathways for deterministically generating complex entangled photonic states.
main_problem: Controlling the g-factors of orbital spin states in quantum dot molecules (QDMs) is essential for achieving high-fidelity generation of multi-photonic cluster states with higher-dimensional entanglement.
main_result: The electron g-factor shows a pronounced step-like change at the tunneling resonance, while the hole g-factor remains nearly constant, demonstrating electric-field control over trion g-factors.
method: Polarization-resolved magneto-photoluminescence spectroscopy was used experimentally, and the results were quantitatively reproduced using an eight-band k.p model theoretically.
model_or_system: The study investigates negatively charged trions (X-) in a single InGaAs QDM, which is composed of two vertically stacked quantum dots separated by about 10 nm, allowing for gate voltage tuning.
key_observables: Electron ($g_e$) and hole ($g_h$) g-factors measured as a function of gate voltage; photoluminescence spectra under magnetic fields.
important_parameters: Gate voltage (electric field), applied magnetic field strength, tunneling resonance voltages, and the trion charge state ($	ext{X}^-$).
main_assumptions: The theoretical model relies on an eight-band k.p approach combined with Configuration Interaction for calculating trion states.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates voltage-dependent PL spectra showing multiple charge states, and a schematic depicts the trion level structure under an in-plane magnetic field (Voigt geometry).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the necessity of g-factor control for quantum state generation. It presents experimental measurements on $	ext{X}^-$ in the QDM, detailing the voltage dependence of $g_e$ and $g_h$. Finally, it validates these findings using an eight-band k.p model to confirm electric-field tunability.
why_interesting: The direct electrical tuning of fundamental parameters like the g-factor in solid-state quantum systems provides a powerful platform for engineering qubit interactions and deterministic entanglement generation protocols relevant to quantum computing architectures.

The insets schematically depict the voltage de- pendent occupation of the orbital states in the trion singlet X− S0. (b) Schematic representation of the trion level structure when applying an in-plane magnetic field (Voigt geometry). (c) Polarization-resolved emission from the trion X− S0 state at B = 7 T and 0.44 V.
